title: Instructor Notes

## About This Course

Essential Digital Skills is a foundation course in practical digital research work. The teaching goal is not to turn participants into policy specialists. It is to help them make better day-to-day decisions about collaboration, governance, data management, interpretation, and responsible AI use.

The four core sessions cover digital tools, digital delivery, governance and policy, and research data management. Broader data interpretation and dedicated AI teaching are separate follow-on courses.

The course works best when learners leave with:

- a clearer mental model of the university research ecosystem
- better judgement about where work should live and how it should be documented
- stronger awareness of risk, roles, and escalation points
- reusable habits they can apply immediately in their own projects

## Recommended Teaching Approach

- Keep teaching blocks short and concrete.
- Prioritise scenario-based discussion over long stretches of exposition.
- Ask learners to map each concept to a live project, role, or workflow.
- Treat the course as workflow design, not compliance theatre.
- Use debriefs to convert broad principles into next-week actions.

## Delivery Pattern

Most sessions in this course already follow a useful rhythm:

1. Short concept framing.
2. Example or comparison.
3. Group activity or reflection task.
4. Debrief focused on practical decisions.

Maintain that pattern where possible. Learners often understand the concept more clearly after they have had to defend a choice, rank a risk, or improve a weak example.

## Session-Level Emphasis

### Digital tools

Use [Digital Tools](../episodes/01-digital_tools.qmd) to clarify the role of Microsoft 365, SharePoint, RIS, UniCore, ORCID, and basic digital security practices. Learners often know these systems exist but not how they fit together.

The lesson also includes literature discovery/reference management and writing tools. Allow **120 minutes overall**, including a 10-minute break after Digital Security. All six topics use 10 minutes teaching. The original four topics each have one five-minute activity; each new topic has three five-minute tasks. This totals 60 minutes teaching and 50 minutes activities, including room debriefs.

Before delivery:

- Check library access and prepare two accessible references for anyone whose search or access fails.
- Test one EndNote or Zotero setup, including importing, duplicate checks, Word citations and export. Demonstrate one tool fully; point out the equivalent workflow in the other.
- Prepare a separate practice library, a duplicate example and a copy of the fictional writing draft with its table already inserted. Share the draft before the writing activity so learners can begin without retyping it. Keep demonstrations separate from live research libraries and documents.
- Check desktop Word captions, cross-references, tracked changes and an available version history. Offer the LaTeX route to existing users rather than requiring beginners to install it.
- Pair learners so one operates and one checks, then swap. Collect actual outputs: a search log, checked references, a reading note, a cited paragraph, an export and a reviewed document.
- Use the stated show-of-hands prompts and short reports from pairs to involve the room. Collect an unresolved access issue rather than spending the activity installing software.

Use a visible five-minute timer for each task and keep reports brief. Treat the first new task as the start of each pair's workflow so they can reuse their output in the next task. Duplicate resolution, a second citation, export round-trip checks and independent renumbering are follow-up practice if they do not fit the room activity.

The writing block includes two brief AI slides derived from the separate AI course. The invented rewrite works without AI accounts or uploading research material; debrief changes in meaning, unsupported claims, verification and recording the contribution.

### Delivery and coordination

Use [Digital Delivery](../episodes/02-digital_delivery.qmd) to make project planning feel lighter and more actionable. The aim is not to impose formal agile doctrine, but to give teams language for iteration, coordination, and shared ownership.

### Governance and policy

Use [Data Governance & Policy](../episodes/03-data_governance_and_policy.qmd) to distinguish ethics, lawful basis, data classification, and institutional compliance. Learners often collapse these into one vague idea of "policy".

### Research data management

Use [Research Data Management](../episodes/04-research_data_managment.qmd) to connect DMPs, folder structures, metadata, storage, retention, and FAIR reuse. Keep bringing the discussion back to actual files, responsibilities, and workflows.

## Optional Follow-on Teaching

Dedicated AI teaching now sits in [Responsible Use of Generative AI](../../responsible_use_of_generative_ai/index.qmd). If learners want deeper coverage of prompting, validation, documentation, and defensible AI use, that course is the natural follow-on.

Data collection, exploration, interpretation and impact belong to [Methods for Data Science](../../methods_for_data_science/index.qmd). Keep these routes separate from the core EDS session list. Use [learner additional material](../learners/additional_material.qmd) to consolidate the four taught themes without adding new prerequisites.

## Common Sticking Points

- Confusion between governance principles and operational decisions.
- Assuming consent solves all data protection questions.
- Treating DMPs as proposal paperwork rather than live workflow planning.
- Underestimating documentation and metadata needs.
- Treating AI fluency as evidence or authority.
- Unclear boundaries between personal working storage and collaborative storage.
- Limited understanding of who owns which decision in a project.

## Facilitation Moves That Usually Help

- Ask learners to justify tool/storage choices against risk level.
- Use “what would you do next week?” prompts to force concrete planning.
- Surface trade-offs explicitly (openness vs sensitivity, speed vs rigor).
- Ask "what would another team member need to know to use this safely?"
- Push groups from abstract principles to named platforms, roles, and actions.
- When an answer is vague, ask what document, system, or person would hold that decision in reality.
- Turn comparison tasks into ranking tasks where possible. Ranking forces prioritisation.

## Managing Policy Questions

Learners will often ask for definitive answers about institutional policy. When the answer depends on context:

- be honest about uncertainty
- distinguish principle from local implementation
- signpost the relevant service or approval route
- avoid improvising a confident answer when escalation is the right move

This is particularly important for:

- ethics approval thresholds
- personal and special category data
- external sharing and cloud services
- retention and preservation decisions
- AI use with sensitive or unpublished material

## Room Setup and Activity Design

- Mixed-role groups usually work well because they expose different assumptions.
- If the room is quiet, start with individual reflection before group discussion.
- If the room is very mixed in confidence, ask pairs to nominate a reporter rather than relying on open plenary discussion.
- Encourage groups to write down one recommended action and one unresolved question after each activity.

## Good Evidence of Learning

You are looking for learners who can:

- explain why a tool or storage choice is appropriate
- identify when a governance issue needs escalation
- improve a weak DMP or documentation example
- check a citation against its source and improve a weak reading note
- propose a small, realistic workflow improvement
- describe AI use in terms of task, source boundary, and verification

## Follow-Up Suggestions

If you have time at the end of a session, ask learners to leave with one sentence in each of these forms:

- "We should stop..."
- "We should start..."
- "We should clarify..."

This produces better follow-up actions than a generic "Any questions?" close.
